name: Frederick Douglass
info: Frederick Douglass (c. 1818–1895) was an American abolitionist, orator, writer and statesman who escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838, wrote three autobiographies and became the leading figure of the African-American civil rights movement of the 19th century.

facts.born: c. February 1818 (he celebrated 14 February) in Talbot County, Maryland, into slavery, as Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey; son of Harriet Bailey, an enslaved woman, and a white father who may have been her master
facts.died: 20 February 1895 in Washington, D.C., of a heart attack, shortly after a meeting of the National Council of Women; buried in Mount Hope Cemetery, Rochester, New York
facts.role: Abolitionist lecturer (from 1841); editor of the North Star (from 1847), Frederick Douglass' Paper and the New National Era; president of the Freedman's Savings Bank (1874); United States Marshal for the District of Columbia (1877); Recorder of Deeds for the District of Columbia (1881); minister resident and consul-general to Haiti (1889–1891)
facts.known: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845); his oratory, among it "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?" (1852); the North Star; his break with William Lloyd Garrison over the Constitution; his support for women's suffrage at Seneca Falls (1848); recruiting black soldiers for the Union; his meetings with Abraham Lincoln

t: Born into slavery in Maryland, Douglass taught himself to read, fought back against the "slave-breaker" Edward Covey and escaped north by train in 1838.

His Narrative of 1845, his speeches and his newspaper the North Star made him a national leader of the abolitionist movement, and he broke with William Lloyd Garrison by holding that the Constitution could be used against slavery.

After the Civil War he worked for the rights of freed people and of women, held federal offices in Washington and served as minister to Haiti, and he is remembered as the foremost African-American leader of his century.
dyk: Douglass was the most photographed American of the 19th century. He never smiled for the camera, so as not to play into the racist caricature of a happy enslaved person.
ev: Born Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey into slavery in Talbot County, Maryland
Escapes from Baltimore by train in a sailor's uniform, reaches New York in less than 24 hours and marries Anna Murray
Publishes Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave and sails for a lecture tour of Ireland and Britain
Returns to the United States, his freedom bought by British supporters, and starts the North Star in Rochester
Speaks for women's suffrage as the only black person at the Seneca Falls Convention
Publishes the broadside Men of Color to Arms! and confers with Abraham Lincoln on the treatment of black soldiers
Becomes United States Marshal for the District of Columbia, the first person of color named to the post
Dies of a heart attack in Washington, D.C., after a meeting of the National Council of Women

sections.early:
Frederick Douglass was born Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey into slavery in Talbot County, Maryland, on the Eastern Shore of the Chesapeake Bay. He did not know his age; from the records of his owner Aaron Anthony the historian Dickson J. Preston determined that he was born in February 1818, and Douglass chose to celebrate 14 February, remembering that his mother called him her "Little Valentine". His mother, Harriet Bailey, was of African descent; his father, who may have been her master, was apparently white. Separated from his mother as an infant, he was raised by his enslaved grandmother Betsy Bailey and saw his mother only a few times before her death when he was seven.

At six he was moved to the Wye House plantation, and after Anthony's death in 1826 he was sent to serve Hugh and Sophia Auld in Baltimore. When he was about twelve Sophia began to teach him the alphabet until her husband objected that literacy would make enslaved people desire freedom; Douglass called it the "first decidedly antislavery lecture" he had heard, and went on teaching himself in secret, helped by The Columbian Orator. In 1833 Thomas Auld sent him to Edward Covey, a farmer known as a "slave-breaker", who whipped him so often that his wounds had little time to heal. At 16 Douglass fought back and won, and Covey never tried to beat him again: "You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man."
sections.rise:
Hired out as a ship caulker in Fell's Point, Baltimore, in 1835, Douglass met Anna Murray, a free black woman, in 1837. On 3 September 1838 he escaped by boarding a northbound train in a sailor's uniform she had given him, carrying papers obtained from a free black seaman, and reached the safe house of David Ruggles in New York City in less than 24 hours. He and Anna married on 15 September and settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts, where Nathan Johnson suggested the surname Douglass from Walter Scott's The Lady of the Lake.

He became a licensed preacher of the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church in 1839 and read William Lloyd Garrison's The Liberator. In 1841, unexpectedly invited to speak, he told his story at the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society's convention in Nantucket and became an anti-slavery lecturer. On the Hundred Conventions tour of 1843 a mob in Pendleton, Indiana, beat him and broke his hand. His Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845) became an immediate bestseller, reprinted nine times within three years, though some skeptics questioned whether a black man could have written it. Fearing that Hugh Auld would try to reclaim him, his friends urged him to tour Ireland and Britain, where he lectured for two years; in 1846 supporters led by Anna Richardson and her sister-in-law Ellen raised funds to buy his freedom from Thomas Auld.
sections.deeds:
Back in the United States in 1847, Douglass used £500 from English supporters to start the North Star in Rochester, New York, under the motto "Right is of no Sex". He and his wife lodged more than four hundred fugitive slaves in their home. In 1848 he was the only black person at the Seneca Falls Convention, where he spoke for Elizabeth Cady Stanton's resolution on women's suffrage, saying he could not accept the vote as a black man if women could not claim it; the resolution passed. On 5 July 1852, in Corinthian Hall in Rochester, he gave the address known as "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?", which one biographer called "perhaps the greatest antislavery oration ever given".

He met John Brown several times, and Brown wrote his Provisional Constitution while staying with him, but in 1859 Douglass declined to join the raid on Harpers Ferry, warning Brown that he was "going into a perfect steel trap". Nearly arrested on a Virginia warrant afterwards, he fled to Canada and went on to England. In the Civil War he urged that black men be allowed to fight for their freedom, published the broadside Men of Color to Arms! on 21 March 1863 and saw his sons Charles and Lewis join the 54th Massachusetts Infantry Regiment. He conferred with President Abraham Lincoln in 1863 on the treatment of black soldiers and in 1864 on how the enslaved of the Confederate states could contribute to the war effort.
sections.opponents:
Douglass met violence from the start: white shipyard workers in Baltimore abused him, he was thrown off a segregated Eastern Railroad train at Lynn in 1841, and mobs attacked him on tour. His break around 1847 with Garrison, who held the Constitution to be pro-slavery, became one of the abolitionist movement's most notable divisions, and radical abolitionists criticized his readiness to talk with slave owners; he replied: "I would unite with anybody to do right and with nobody to do wrong."

After the war he split with the faction of the women's movement led by Stanton by supporting the 15th Amendment, which gave the vote to black men only; Stanton argued that women and black men should fight together for universal suffrage, while Douglass feared that linking the causes would defeat both. In 1876, at the unveiling of the Emancipation Memorial, he called Lincoln "the white man's President" and criticized his tardiness on emancipation, while saying that measured by the sentiment of his country Lincoln was "swift, zealous, radical, and determined". He opposed the Exodusters and the Back-to-Africa movement and was booed by some audiences for it.

His marriage in 1884 to Helen Pitts, a white suffragist nearly 20 years younger, provoked a storm of controversy; his children considered it a repudiation of their mother. His relationship with Ottilie Assing caused recurring speculation; Blight concludes that they "were probably lovers", though the surviving letters contain no proof.
sections.last:
During Reconstruction Douglass supported Ulysses S. Grant, started his last newspaper, the New National Era, in 1870, and accompanied a commission to the West Indies on the annexation of Santo Domingo, which he favoured and Congress opposed. In 1872 he was nominated without his knowledge as Victoria Woodhull's running mate on the Equal Rights Party ticket, the first African American nominated for vice president, and that June his house in Rochester burned down, arson being suspected; he moved to Washington, D.C. He became president of the Freedman's Savings Bank in March 1874, a few months before it went bankrupt.

Rutherford B. Hayes made him United States Marshal for the District of Columbia in 1877, and in 1881 he became Recorder of Deeds. In 1877 he visited his former enslaver Thomas Auld on his deathbed, and the two men reconciled. Anna died in 1882. In 1888 he became the first African American to receive a vote for president in a major party's roll call. From 1889 he was minister resident and consul-general to Haiti, resigning in July 1891 when it became apparent that President Benjamin Harrison meant to gain permanent access to Haitian territory regardless of that country's desires.

On 20 February 1895, after receiving a standing ovation at a meeting of the National Council of Women, he returned home and died of a heart attack. Thousands passed his coffin, and he was buried beside Anna in Mount Hope Cemetery in Rochester, where he had lived for 25 years.
sections.legacy:
Douglass has been called "the most important leader of the movement for African-American civil rights in the 19th century". Abolitionists of his time described him as a living counterexample to the claim that enslaved people lacked the intellectual capacity to function as independent citizens. His three autobiographies, the Narrative (1845), My Bondage and My Freedom (1855) and Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1881, revised 1892), promoted the cause of abolition, and Charles H. T. Lesch describes his political thought as "natural rights from below", drawn from the experience of the enslaved. He supported equal rights for women, immigrants and the poor, and in 1869 defended Chinese immigration when many fellow Republicans opposed it.

Roy Finkenbine calls him "the most influential African American of the nineteenth century", who made a career of agitating the American conscience; less than a month before his death Douglass advised a young man: "Agitate! Agitate! Agitate!" David W. Blight writes that he very much wished to see himself as a founder and defender of the "Second American Republic" that came out of the Civil War; Blight's biography won the Pulitzer Prize for History in 2019.

A statue unveiled in Rochester in 1899 made him the first African American so memorialized in the country. His home at Cedar Hill is the Frederick Douglass National Historic Site, the Episcopal Church remembers him on 20 February, and schools, bridges, stamps and Rochester's airport bear his name.

summary: Frederick Douglass (c. 1818–1895) escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became a national leader of the abolitionist movement through his speeches, his newspaper the North Star and his autobiographies. He supported women's suffrage, recruited black soldiers in the Civil War and later held federal offices and served as minister to Haiti.
notes: Birth: Douglass's own final estimate was 1817; Dickson J. Preston's dating from Aaron Anthony's records is February 1818, and the article's lead gives c. February 14, 1818. start 1818, circa true.
Marriage: 15 September 1838, which the article calls 'just eleven days after Douglass had reached New York'; only the date is given.
Religious views (the 'Christianity of Christ' and the 'Christianity of America', the 1852 charge of 'blasphemy' against pro-slavery ministers) were cut from 'opponents' for length.
The article says the 1846 purchase of his freedom was from Thomas Auld, though Hugh Auld is named as the ex-owner his friends feared; both kept as the article has them.
The 1877 'first person of color' claim is kept to the event, not repeated in 'last'.
The Garrison split: the article dates it 'around 1847' and his public change of view to the 1851 speech; 'around 1847' is used.
Julia Griffiths is named in the article alongside Assing but without detail; only Assing is named in the section.

Left out for space: the Freeland Sabbath school, the Narrative's translations, Scotland and the violin, the 1848 letter to Thomas Auld, school desegregation, the Chambersburg quarry meeting in detail and Shields Green, the 1867 'three boxes' speech, the Santo Domingo quarrel with Charles Sumner, Douglass Place in Baltimore, the 1886-1887 tour, the many recent commemorations.
